doc.title: Paul Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Lessons with Royal Brown and the goal of studio work
summary: Lessons from age eight with city organist Royal Brown, technical work plus pop books; even at 14 he wanted to be a studio player.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Not Paderewski, but — so they thought well maybe he’s got a little talent. And between the two of them I should have. And they gave me lessons starting at eight. I took lessons from the time I was eight until sixteen, and at sixteen I just kind of went on my own from there on. And the teacher I owe most of it to I mean was a guy named Royal Brown who was the city organist at San Diego. And I used to take a lesson after he got through with his afternoon concerts. He used to play “The Well Tempered Clavichord” [Clavier] and all these kind of things, all the Bach stuff. He was a master of Bach on a five manual organ at Balboa Park on Wednesdays Saturdays and Sundays, and then once a week I would meet him in the back there, either there or at his house depending on what day I took my lesson, and he would give me a real legit 45 minute lesson. He would never play anything for me, because I was born with a photographic mind so that if he played something for me I didn’t have to read it, I could play it back at him.
Did he discover this up front, where you demonstrated that ability and he decided that’s not what we need here.
Yeah. Because strangely enough at the age of about 14 I knew what I wanted to do. I didn’t want to sit in a nightclub and play jazz. I wanted to be in the studios.

That was my main goal in life. And I made it, in about 1950 I got into my first studio thing and I stayed in the studios for about 20 years. But he was very smart, he let me play 45 minutes of all the technical stuff, the Hanon and Czerny and all this and the Bach and Mozart, it was mostly technical stuff. He never pushed me into learning by rote or either way, the Rachmaninoff and the heavy stuff that you have to spend weeks and weeks and weeks before you can play the thing. And he just worked on my facility and then the last 15 minutes he’d let me play my pop books, which was very smart of him. And I had Nat Cole and Tatum and Eddie Duchin, and all the pianists of the day at the time, you know Tatum of course is all our Gods, and there’s never been and I don’t think there will ever be another man with two right hands.
